parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: In the Bohr model, the n=2 electron-orbit radius is four times the n=1 radius. What is v₂/v₁? A. 1/4  B. 1/2  C. 2  D. 4

answer.text: Official answer B; editorial worked explanation: Coulomb attraction supplies centripetal force: ke²/r² = mv²/r, so v² = ke²/(mr) and v is proportional to 1/√r. Therefore v₂/v₁ = √(r₁/r₂) = √(1/4) = 1/2.
answer.evidence: Official May 2023 Physics HL Paper 1 TZ1 answer grid checked on PDF page 3; explanation independently calculated from the visible source question.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Which statement about atomic nuclei is correct? Nuclear density is: A. directly proportional to mass number  B. inversely proportional to nuclear radius  C. inversely proportional to volume  D. constant for all nuclei

answer.text: Official answer D; editorial worked explanation: Nuclear radius follows R = R₀A¹ᐟ³, so nuclear volume is proportional to R³ and hence to A. Nuclear mass is also approximately proportional to A. Their ratio, density = mass/volume, is therefore approximately constant.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 5.0 MeV approaches a heavy nucleus head-on. Treat the nucleus as fixed and the interaction as Coulomb repulsion until the alpha particle turns at a centre-to-centre distance of 1.61×10⁻¹⁴ m. The nucleus has nucleon number A=58. Use Eₖ=2kZe²/d, k=8.99×10⁹ N m² C⁻², e=1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 MeV=1.602×10⁻¹³ J and nuclear radius R=(1.2×10⁻¹⁵ m)×∛A. (a) Find the proton number Z. (b) Find the closest-approach distance as a multiple of the nuclear radius. (c) Explain whether replacing the target by an isotope with the same proton number but different neutron number changes the turning distance in this model.

answer.text: (a) Z=Eₖd/(2ke²)≈27.95, so Z=28. (b) R=(1.2×10⁻¹⁵ m)×∛58≈4.65×10⁻¹⁵ m, and d/R≈3.47, about 3.5. (c) It does not change: the nuclear charge and incident energy are unchanged, so the Coulomb turning distance is unchanged in the fixed-target approximation.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: For a 5.0 MeV alpha particle approaching a particular heavy nucleus head-on, the Coulomb turning distance is about 3.5 nuclear radii. (a) Explain why increasing the alpha energy sufficiently can produce deviations from the point-charge Rutherford-scattering model. (b) Estimate the energy at which the calculated turning distance becomes one nuclear radius. Assume the target remains fixed and use turning distance inversely proportional to incident kinetic energy.

answer.text: (a) Higher-energy alpha particles approach more closely. Near the nuclear radius, the finite charge distribution and short-range nuclear interaction become relevant, so a purely point-charge Coulomb model is no longer adequate. (b) Reducing the turning distance by a factor 3.5 requires increasing the energy by 3.5: E≈3.5×5.0=17.5 MeV, approximately 17 MeV using unrounded radii.

fast-duplicate-followup-bohr-radius-spee.hint: Relate orbital speed to radius using Coulomb attraction as the centripetal force, or compare the Bohr angular-momentum expressions for the two states.
notes: The stated radius ratio is four; speed is inversely proportional to the square root of orbital radius in the Bohr model.
When using quantized angular momentum, include the change from n=1 to n=2 as well as the change in radius.

fast-ib-a6e5d76baf5090c2-39:whole.hint: Combine how nuclear mass and nuclear volume each scale with nucleon number A.
notes: The relation R ∝ A¹ᐟ³ implies R³ ∝ A, so a nucleus's volume grows in direct proportion to nucleon number.
Because each nucleon has nearly the same mass, nuclear mass also scales with A; equal scaling in numerator and denominator makes density nearly constant.

original-ib26mc2-written-7-a-bi-bii:whol.hint: At the turning point all initial kinetic energy has become electric potential energy. Distinguish proton number from the nucleon number used in the radius model.
notes: The alpha particle has charge +2e. Missing that factor of two would give an incorrect target proton number.
The isotope can have a different nuclear radius, but that does not alter a turning distance still outside the nucleus in this point-charge, fixed-target model.

original-ib26mc2-written-7-ci-cii:whole.hint: Identify which assumption fails when the projectile gets close to the nucleus. Use an inverse proportion for the energy estimate.
notes: Rutherford scattering treats the charge as concentrated at a point for the distances being probed. Deviations at small distances provide information about nuclear size.
This is an order-of-magnitude boundary for the model, not a sharp universal onset energy. Use the same head-on and fixed-target assumptions for the scaling.

cross-aq24p2-20:whole.hint: Compare how nuclear mass and nuclear volume depend on nucleon number.
notes: Nuclear radius is approximately R = R₀A^(1/3), while nuclear mass is approximately proportional to A. Volume therefore scales with A.
A is nucleon number and Z is proton number; neutron number is A − Z. Do not confuse the radius of the nucleus with the much larger atomic radius.
